acts.title: Text A · Four labels, applied by other people
text: Born between roughly 1946 and 1964, the baby boomers are usually described as optimistic, competitive and willing to work very long hours. Having entered the workforce when jobs were plentiful, they tend to expect loyalty in both directions.

Generation X, born in the following two decades, is the group most often called realistic and independent. Raised in the first period when both parents commonly worked, they are described as family-focused and critical of authority — a combination that sounds contradictory and is not.
Generation Y, also known as millennials, has a reputation for being arrogant and self-centred. Having grown up with the internet, they are also, by every measure, the most open-minded of the four.
Generation Z, born into the smartphone, is the hardest to characterize, mostly because the people writing the descriptions are not in it.

items.q: What is Text A doing?
o: Setting out how four generations are usually described
Arguing that generations do not exist

items.q: What does the writer note about Generation Z?
o: It is hardest to describe because the describers are outside it

acts.title: Text B · What the labels are actually measuring
text: Read carefully, most generational descriptions turn out to be descriptions of age rather than of a generation.

Being twenty-five and being described as self-centred have gone together for a very long time. Surveys conducted in 1968 found older people complaining, in almost identical language, about the group now filing the same complaint.

The second problem is economics. Having entered the workforce during a recession, a person behaves cautiously with money for the rest of their life, whatever decade they were born in. That is not a personality; it is a scar.

None of this makes the labels useless. Used carefully, they are a rough shorthand for shared experience. Used carelessly — and they usually are — they become a stereotype, applied to seventy million people at once and true of almost none of them.

items.s: The writer argues that many generational traits are really age effects.
Surveys in 1968 found older people saying similar things about the young.
The writer says entering work during a recession has lifelong effects.
The writer concludes that the labels are entirely useless.
The writer thinks the labels are usually used carefully.

acts.title: Look again at the two texts
text: Born between 1946 and 1964, the baby boomers are usually described as optimistic.
Having entered the workforce when jobs were plentiful, they expect loyalty.
Raised in the first period when both parents worked, they are family-focused.
Having grown up with the internet, they are the most open-minded of the four.
Read carefully, most generational descriptions turn out to describe age.
Used carelessly, they become a stereotype.

items.q: “Born between 1946 and 1964, the baby boomers…” — what is the full form?
“Having entered the workforce…, they expect loyalty.” What does having + participle add?
o: That this happened before the main verb

items.q: “Used carelessly, they become a stereotype.” Who or what is used?
o: They — the labels. The subject must be the same in both halves

items.q: Why do writers use these clauses at all?
o: They shorten a relative or time clause without losing meaning

acts.title: Participle clauses: the short form of a longer clause
rule: A participle clause is a relative clause or a time clause with the subject and the auxiliary removed. It is not decoration: it is how written English keeps long sentences readable. The one rule that governs everything is that the missing subject must be the subject of the main clause.
points: Replaces an active clause: the man who lives above me → the man living above me.
Replaces a passive clause: the labels which are used carelessly → the labels used carelessly.
Says the action came first: having grown up with the internet, they are open-minded.
A participle clause at the front is followed by a comma and describes the subject of what follows.
If the subjects differ, the sentence says something absurd. Walking to work, the rain started is wrong — the rain was not walking.
eg: The man living above me plays loud music.
= who lives. Present participle, active.
The labels used carelessly become stereotypes.
= which are used. Past participle, passive.
Born in 1958, she remembers the first landing.
= who was born. Past participle at the front.
Having entered work in a recession, he is cautious with money.
The entering came first.
Read carefully, the descriptions are about age.
= if they are read carefully.
Feeling tired, I went to bed early.
= because I felt tired.
Anybody wanting a ticket should come early.
= who wants. Very common in notices.
Written in 1968, the survey found the same complaint.
Past participle, front position.
Walking to work, I saw the fire.
Correct — I was walking and I saw.
Having locked the door, she realized her keys were inside.
Correct — she locked and she realized.
acts.careful: Check the subject before you use a front participle clause. “Walking to work, the rain started” says the rain was walking to work. If the thing doing the participle is not the subject of the main clause, rewrite the sentence in full.

acts.title: From relative clause to participle, in three moves
steps: The labels which are used carelessly become stereotypes.
Start with the full relative clause.
The labels … used carelessly become stereotypes.
The labels used carelessly become stereotypes.
2 · Delete the auxiliary: are. The participle stays.
The people who live above me → the people living above me.
3 · For an ACTIVE clause, the verb becomes -ing instead.
Having entered work in a recession, he is cautious.
4 · If the action came first, use having + past participle.

items.q: The survey which was written in 1968 → The survey ___ in 1968.
Anybody who wants a ticket → Anybody ___ a ticket.
Because he had grown up with the internet, he is open-minded. → ___ up with the internet, he is open-minded.
Which pair of words is deleted when you shorten a passive relative clause?
o: The pronoun and the form of be

lines: The man [living|lived|who living] above me plays loud music.
The labels [used|using|which using] carelessly become stereotypes.
[Born|Being born of|Bearing] in 1958, she remembers the first landing.
[Having|Have|Been] entered work in a recession, he is cautious with money.
Anybody [wanting|wanted|who wanting] a ticket should come early, and the survey [written|writing|which writing] in 1968 said the same thing.

write.q: Write about 180 words describing a generation you know well — your own, your parents’, or the one just behind you — and then say where the description breaks down. Use at least two front participle clauses with a comma, at least one having + past participle, and one participle clause replacing a relative clause. Check the subject of every participle before you finish.
plan: what they are usually described as
one thing that is genuinely true
write.model:
Born in the late 1980s in a country that changed its name while they were at primary school, my generation here is usually described as pragmatic, and that is the polite word for it.

Having grown up in the years when nobody’s salary arrived on time, we are, almost without exception, strange about money. People raised in that decade keep cash in the flat. They will explain, at length, why this is rational.

The part that is genuinely true is a suspicion of institutions. Anybody promising a guaranteed return gets a flat no, and I think that instinct has saved most of us at least once.

Where the label fails is everything else. Described as cautious, half the people I studied with left for jobs in cities they had never visited. Described as materialistic, the same people give away more than my parents ever did. The generation is a real thing. The personality attached to it is not.
